planting.note: Set out container-grown or bare-root plants in early spring in well-drained, acidic soil; site a second genetically distinct chinquapin nearby, since nut set is far better with cross-pollination even though the species carries both flower types.

directions: Rush is a long-cultivated selection of the native American chinquapin, picked out generations ago for producing a noticeably heavier and more dependable nut crop than typical wild plants of this thicket-forming shrub-to-small-tree species. The small, sweet, thin-shelled nuts ripen in burs in fall and have a richer flavor than most chestnuts, making the plant a favorite among nut collectors despite its modest size. It tolerates dry, sandy, infertile soils far better than Chinese or American chestnut and suckers readily from the base, so remove excess shoots if a single-trunk form is wanted. Because chinquapin wood and bark are susceptible to the same blight that devastated American chestnut, keep plants in full sun with good air movement to reduce disease pressure.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in early spring in light, well-drained, acidic soil and give it full sun; pair with a second chinquapin selection or wild seedling within a couple hundred feet for reliable cross-pollination and fuller bur set.

directions: Fuller is an older named selection of American chinquapin recognized alongside 'Rush' as one of the improved clones grown for larger, more consistent nut crops than seedling-grown wild plants. Like the species, it forms a multi-stemmed, suckering shrub or small tree with narrow, toothed, glossy leaves and spiny burs that split open in autumn to release one or two small, glossy, sweet nuts. It bears at a younger age than most chestnuts and crops heavily in good years, but individual plants are not reliably self-fruitful, so interplanting with a second clone improves yields. Give it the same dry, sandy, acidic woodland-edge conditions chinquapins favor in the wild, and avoid heavy, poorly drained soils.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, spacing widely to allow the broad mature crown to develop; include a second chestnut cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Tsukuba is a widely grown Japanese chestnut cultivar from Japan's national chestnut breeding program, which dates to the late 1940s, prized for producing large, glossy nuts with good storage quality on a reliably productive tree. It bears earlier in life than many chestnut cultivars and crops consistently once established, with burs splitting in early autumn to drop nuts over several weeks. The tree needs full sun and well-drained, acidic soil, and like other Japanese chestnuts it shows useful resistance to chestnut blight, making it a common breeding parent as well as an orchard tree. Harvest promptly after bur drop and refrigerate nuts quickly, since sugars convert fast and quality fades within days at room temperature.
sources: NARO Institute of Fruit Tree and Tea Science

planting.note: Set grafted trees in spring in full sun and deep, acidic, well-drained soil; allow ample room for a wide mature crown and plant a compatible cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Ginyose is a traditional Japanese chestnut cultivar dating to 1753, when the grower Kanuemon Oku brought seed from Hiroshima Prefecture to Kura-gaki Village in Settsu Province, and it has since been maintained as a named clone through grafting. It produces medium to large nuts with the mild sweetness typical of Japanese chestnut, on a vigorous tree that adapts to a range of soils as long as drainage is good. Growers value it for dependable annual bearing and long regional history, and it remains a reference cultivar in Japanese chestnut breeding and genetic diversity studies. Thin out crowded burs in heavy-crop years to keep nut size consistent, and harvest promptly once burs begin splitting to avoid losses to wildlife.
sources: NARO Institute of Fruit Tree and Tea Science
DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ) genome release

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and deep, acidic, well-drained soil, siting a second chestnut cultivar nearby for pollination; give it room since mature trees form a broad, spreading crown.

directions: Porotan was bred by crossing the line '550-40' with 'Tanzawa' and released in 2006 by Japan's national agricultural research organization as the first Japanese chestnut cultivar with an easy-peeling inner pellicle, solving the main drawback of the species compared with European and Chinese chestnuts. Roasted nuts separate cleanly from both the outer shell and the papery inner skin with little effort, making this cultivar especially popular for home roasting and processing rather than raw eating. The tree otherwise grows and crops much like other Japanese chestnuts, bearing burs of two to three nuts that split open in early autumn. Because the easy-peeling trait is a genetic trademark of this specific clone, propagate it only by grafting rather than from seed to keep the characteristic true.
sources: NARO Institute of Fruit Tree and Tea Science
